newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: PM GIVES FISCHER LEEWAY ON NATIVE TITLE SUPPORT
It's believed the Prime Minister has given his deputy, Tim Fischer, some leeway to fight for the National Party's position against his ten point plan on native title.
While John Howard firmly believes his plan is the right one, it's believed the strategy aims to ease the increased party pressure on Mr Fischer.
The National Party Federal Management Committee met yesterday and determined Mr Howard's plan unacceptable because it fails to wipe out native title on pastoral leases.
The Committee says National M-Ps have a right and duty to seek changes to the plan.

The move allows Mr Fischer to articulate his party's position unconstrained by the differences between the Coalition parties. He will, however, be expected to support the Cabinet's final decision on the matter.
QLD PREMIER AND CENTURY ZINC BOSS PRAISE RAY ROBINSON
The Queensland Premier and Century Zinc's general manager have paid tribute to ATSIC deputy chairman Ray Robinson for his role in getting the go-ahead for the billion-dollar mining project.

Century Zinc and Queensland's state Cabinet will meet today to rubber stamp the far north-west Queensland Century Zinc project, after it was finally given the go-ahead late yesterday. The Queensland Premier, Rob Borbidge, looked delighted when he emerged from a meeting with native title and Century Zinc representatives to announce an historic agreement had finally been reached.
Mr Robinson was instrumental in obtaining unanimous agreement from the 12 native title claimants.
MOORE SAYS BED TAX THE WORST SINCE '89
The Federal Tourism Minister, John Moore, has described the 10-percent bed tax as the biggest blow to tourism since the 1989 pilots strike.
Mr Moore says the move is completely rgressive, particularly in the lead-up to the Sydney Olympics.
He's called on the New South Wales government to immediately withdraw the tax.
TWO MEN CONVICTED OVER EXPORTING OF FOSSILS
Two men will be sentenced in Perth later this week for their part in a scheme to export valuable Australian fossils for sale in Germany and Japan.

David Edward Vaughan, from Western Australia, and Edward Dudley Madden, of South Australia, were both convicted of charges relating to the export of fossils with an estimated age of up to 650-million years.
The District Court in Perth was told that Vaughan and Madden had been involved in the removal of a protected fossil from a National Park in South Australia's Flinders Ranges.
Vaughan had also organised the export of other fossils, taken from Western Australia's far north.
The prosecution has called for Vaughan to be jailed, while it said a suspended sentence or fine would be an appropriate penalty for Madden.
EARTH TREMOR HITS NORTH TASMANIA
Parts of North Tasmania have been were shaken by an earth tremor on Tuesday evening.

The University of Tasmania's Geology Department says the tremor, which measured three-point-five on the richter scale, struck 35 kilometres west-north west of Launceston, near the township of Frankford.
The department's Dr Michael Roach says the tremor struck at three past six this evening.
Dr Roach says he's had no reports of any structural damage, although he says any such damage would be light.
